clue.text: Asteroid in Pisces

parts.note: zoologists class the sea creature as an asteroid, and the clue jokingly files a star-shaped one among the fishes of the zodiac sign

explanation.surface: An astronomer spots a minor planet in the constellation of the Fishes.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is astronomy; in fact Asteroidea is the zoological class of the five-armed sea creature, and Pisces means fishes.
explanation.definitionFit: Asteroidea is the scientific class of these echinoderms, so one is literally an asteroid living in the sea.

clue.text: Cast, say, from end to end

indicators.note: say signals that the word for cast is spoken, giving a word of the same sound but different spelling

parts.note: to cast a stone is to throw it

explanation.surface: An angler or actor is told to cast from one end to the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Passing from end to end of something is going all the way across it, a preposition of complete passage.

clue.text: It makes a good martinet if a poor angler

definitions.text: It makes a good martinet if a poor angler

parts.words: It makes a good martinet if a poor angler
parts.note: a strict disciplinarian is said to rule with this, while a metal fishing pole would be useless for catching fish

explanation.surface: A remark that the same person may be a fine disciplinarian but a hopeless fisherman.
explanation.walkthrough: To rule with a rod of iron is the idiom for harsh discipline; a rod made of iron would be far too heavy and stiff for fishing.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom ruling with an unbending metal rod describes a tyrannical disciplinarian, which is what a martinet is.

clue.text: One can hold me up as a coming theatrical type

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: hold means the first pair of words contain the next piece within them

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word me is read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A performer boasts that anyone can lift them up as a rising stage figure.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'up' reverses, and 'hold' signals a container. The definition alludes to Eugene O'Neill's play The Iceman Cometh, so the character is one who is 'coming'.
explanation.definitionFit: Eugene O'Neill's play The Iceman Cometh is named for an awaited figure, so he is a theatrical type who is coming.

clue.text: Standardized industry-agriculture association

parts.note: a pairing of a factory tool with a farm tool, displayed on a flag or standard of the Soviet Union

explanation.surface: Sounds like a formal body that sets common rules for industry and farming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standardized' means put on a standard, i.e. a flag: the Soviet flag joins symbols of industry (a tool for metal) and agriculture (a tool for reaping).
explanation.definitionFit: The Soviet emblem joined a worker's tool and a peasant's tool, symbolising the union of industry and agriculture, and it was flown on the standard.

clue.text: Wood about right for rear, part of gun

indicators.note: about means the wood goes around the next piece

parts.note: beech is a kind of wood

explanation.surface: Timber wrapped around a right-hand piece forms the back end of a firearm.
explanation.definitionFit: The rear section of a gun barrel, where the charge is loaded, is the breech; the word also once meant the buttocks.

clue.text: Sounded bully for Wordsworth's Peter, having money due to him

parts.note: Peter Bell is the title character of a poem by William Wordsworth
someone who has money due to them is owed it

explanation.surface: Someone shouted 'bully for you' at Wordsworth's character, a creditor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sounded bully' means made a noise like a bull, not cheered 'bully for him'.
explanation.definitionFit: A bull roars loudly, so to sound like one is to roar or shout deeply.

clue.text: Loan he asked (Antony) to assign to a purpose

parts.note: in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar the speaker begs 'lend me your ears', asking for a loan of them
Mark Antony, Roman general in Julius Caesar

explanation.surface: Mark Antony asked for a loan, which must be allocated to some purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed name tells you whose request: Mark Antony's speech opens 'Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears'.
explanation.definitionFit: To set funds aside for a particular use is to earmark them, from marking livestock's ears to show ownership.

clue.text: Some joints hold, oddly, a crop of old wine

indicators.note: hold means the joints contain the rearranged letters

parts.note: hips are joints of the body

indicators.note: oddly signals that the letters of a crop are put in a strange order

explanation.surface: An image of hips holding, strangely, a harvest of vintage wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' looks like a comment on the joints but is the anagram signal; 'hold' is the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Hippocras was a medieval spiced wine, sweetened and strained through a cloth bag, so an old wine.

clue.text: This rocker all-powerful on Earth

parts.note: the saying goes that the hand that rocks this rules the world

explanation.surface: Seems to describe a rock star who rules the planet.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'the hand that rocks the cradle rules the world' makes the baby's swinging bed the rocker with world power.
explanation.definitionFit: A baby's swinging bed rocks, and the proverb says the hand rocking it rules the world.

clue.text: Partly informal, a proper derangement of epitaphs was her boast

definitions.text: derangement of epitaphs was her boast

indicators.note: Partly says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone casual yet proper boasted of a muddled set of gravestone inscriptions.
explanation.walkthrough: In Sheridan's The Rivals, Mrs Malaprop boasts of 'a nice derangement of epitaphs', meaning arrangement of epithets.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheridan's character in The Rivals garbles words, and her famous line misuses derangement and epitaphs.

clue.text: Gaffer gets us mobilized to vote,

indicators.note: mobilized means the letters are set in motion and rearranged

explanation.surface: The boss gets the staff organised to go out and vote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mobilized' rearranges GAFFER + US.
explanation.definitionFit: Suffrage is the right to vote, so the word stands for the franchise itself.

clue.text: Paper of some size to ring firm about tax return

parts.note: O is shaped like a ring

indicators.note: about means the firm's letters go around the next piece

parts.note: CO is short for company, a firm

indicators.note: return means the tax word is read backwards

parts.note: VAT is value added tax

explanation.surface: Instructions to phone a company about its tax return, on some size of paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' reverses the tax and 'about' wraps the firm round it; octavo is a sheet folded into eight leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Octavo is a book or paper size made by folding a sheet into eight leaves.

clue.text: Jane ditched in London

parts.note: Jane, the mistress of Edward IV, with the word ditch added gives a district in the east of London

explanation.surface: A woman named Jane was dumped somewhere in London.
explanation.walkthrough: Jane Shore was the mistress of Edward IV; add DITCH to her surname and you get Shoreditch, a district of East London.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Shore was a famous royal mistress, and Shoreditch is a London district built from her surname plus ditch.

clue.text: Jewellers talking shop with a bird ?

definitions.text: Jewellers talking shop with a bird

parts.words: Jewellers talking shop with a bird
parts.note: jewellers talking about their gems would be having gem talk, which splits as the name of a small songbird

explanation.surface: Jewellers gossip about their trade with a feathered friend.
explanation.walkthrough: Gem dealers talking shop are having a 'stone chat'; joined up, that is a small songbird.
explanation.definitionFit: The stonechat is a small chat-family songbird whose call sounds like two pebbles knocked together.

clue.text: Play its title role with caution

definitions.meaning: Harold Pinter's 1960 play is named after its title character, a man who looks after a building
read as two words, one who takes care, i.e. acts with caution

explanation.surface: An actor told to play the lead part carefully.
explanation.walkthrough: Harold Pinter's play The Caretaker; split as 'care taker', one who takes care.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinter's play is named for a building's custodian, and split up the word suggests someone who takes care, acting cautiously.

clue.text: Sign for a part Hugo changed

indicators.note: changed signals that these letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Victor Hugo altered part of his work, in return for which he gave a signature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changed' rearranges A PART HUGO.
explanation.definitionFit: A signature written for a fan is an autograph; signing one's name is the act.

clue.text: Spanish aunt in towelling of ancient time

indicators.note: in means the Spanish word sits inside the fabric

parts.note: terry is looped cotton towelling fabric
tia is Spanish for aunt

explanation.surface: A Spanish aunt wrapped in an old-fashioned towel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is the container signal; terry is the looped cotton used for bath towels.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tertiary is a geological period, so the adjective means belonging to a remote prehistoric era.

clue.text: Drink row — a poem about that

indicators.note: about means the poem goes around the other pieces

parts.note: an ode is a lyric poem
a range is a row, as of mountains or houses

explanation.surface: A quarrel breaks out over a drink, and a poem is written about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'row' looks like a quarrel but means a line, as of hills; 'about' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Orangeade is a sweet fizzy soft drink flavoured with citrus fruit.

clue.text: Done any damage ? This will ease the pain

indicators.note: damage signals that the words are knocked out of shape and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks if you have done any harm, then offers a painkiller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'damage' rearranges DONE ANY.
explanation.definitionFit: An anodyne is a painkilling medicine, something that soothes suffering.

clue.text: Men only gambling on the Stock Exchange

definitions.meaning: a party for men only is a stag party, and such gatherings are stag
stock market speculators who buy new share issues to sell quickly at a profit

explanation.surface: A men's club spends its time betting on stocks and shares.
explanation.walkthrough: A stag on the Stock Exchange buys new shares hoping to sell them at once for a profit.
explanation.definitionFit: Male deer gather without females, hence all-male parties, and share speculators are traditionally called by the same name.

clue.text: There's danger in strong drink or meat

indicators.note: in means the danger word sits inside the drink

parts.note: gin is a strong spirit
risk means danger

explanation.surface: A warning that strong liquor, or perhaps meat, is dangerous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is the container signal; the surface warning against liquor hides it. Griskin is the lean part of a pork loin.
explanation.definitionFit: Griskin is a lean cut from the loin of a pig, a regional name for pork.

clue.text: This type of car one's property ?

definitions.meaning: a car with a long body and rear door, the British name for a station wagon
the whole of a person's possessions or landholding

explanation.surface: A question whether a car is the owner's property.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain an estate car is what Americans call a station wagon.
explanation.definitionFit: Estate names both a long-backed car body and someone's total holdings or land.

clue.text: Meredith's Number One character

parts.note: George Meredith wrote a novel titled for a self-centred man, someone who puts number one first

explanation.surface: Seems to name the leading character in a novel by Meredith.
explanation.walkthrough: George Meredith's 1879 novel is The Egoist; 'number one' is oneself, so the character always looks after number one.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone obsessed with self-interest looks after number one, and Meredith's novel of that title portrays Sir Willoughby Patterne.

clue.text: Marks one gains in translation

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: in translation signals that the letters are converted into a new order, with in serving as fodder

explanation.surface: A student loses or gains marks when translating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like part of 'in translation' but is fodder: only 'translation' signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Insignia are badges or emblems, distinguishing marks of rank or office.

clue.text: It ain't much money one piles up on the farm

definitions.text: It ain't much money one piles up on the farm

parts.words: It ain't much money one piles up on the farm
parts.note: slang for a trivial sum of money is the dried grass a farmer stores, and a pile of it is built in the field

explanation.surface: A farmer complains that farming makes little money.
explanation.walkthrough: In American slang, 'that ain't hay' means a sizeable sum, so hay is small money; a pile of hay on a farm is the stack.
explanation.definitionFit: A large pile of dried grass built up in a farmyard for storage.

clue.text: State of cordon bleu bakery

parts.note: a fancy dessert of ice cream in meringue is baked and named after a US state

explanation.surface: Seems to ask about the condition of a fine French bakery.
explanation.walkthrough: Baked Alaska is a dessert of ice cream covered in meringue and briefly baked; 'State' is a US state.
explanation.definitionFit: Baked Alaska is a celebrated chef's dessert, named for the northernmost US state.

clue.text: Fashionable object in test

indicators.note: in means the object word goes inside the test word

parts.note: to try is to test
an end is an aim or object

explanation.surface: A fashionable item being tested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'object' means an aim or goal, not a thing; 'in' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something up-to-date and stylish follows the current trend, so it is in vogue.

clue.text: One always remembered an Alpine crossing in 218 BC

definitions.text: One always remembered an Alpine crossing in 218 BC

parts.words: One always remembered an Alpine crossing in 218 BC
parts.note: this animal is said never to forget, and Hannibal took a herd of them over the Alps in that year

explanation.surface: A veteran recalls crossing the Alps in ancient times.
explanation.walkthrough: Elephants proverbially never forget, and Hannibal marched elephants over the Alps in 218 BC.
explanation.definitionFit: Hannibal's war beasts crossed the Alps, and the proverb says this huge animal never forgets.
